annotations.text:
A · ANSWER FIRST — anchored
Proof before commitment: a worked sample is on screen before you type anything, and the 3D stops being the price of entry. Closest of the five to shipping from the current code.
Tradeoff: a photo hero is still doing the persuading, and a sample invites "but that isn't my building".

B · THE LEDGER — anchored
The result is a page, not a modal, and every assumption sits on it, editable in place. The strongest answer to "why should I believe this number", and naturally linkable.
Tradeoff: cold. No image, no hook — the weakest of the five for a first-time visitor arriving from a social link.

C · CIVIC BULLETIN — stretch
Says the true thing first: you cannot buy this yet, and here is the bill that changes it. Turns a dead end into a reason to come back, and the calculator becomes the personalisation underneath.
Tradeoff: buries the calculator the search traffic came for, and it dates the day the Governor signs.

D · SUN DIAL — stretch
The model becomes the interface. No address, no 600KB download, no six-second wait — the number moves as you turn the dial, and the eight sectors are honest about the 45° snap the code already does.
Tradeoff: a toy until someone enters an address, and the furthest of the five from the current brand.

E · BLOCK MAP — stretch
Answers the question the other four leave open: is my number any good? Leads with the city, and comparison is the thing people actually share.
Tradeoff: much the largest build — it needs precomputed figures for every block before the page can render at all.
The one change everything else follows from: the number arrives BEFORE the 3D, not after it. PLUTO alone (floors, height, footprint) is enough to answer in about a second.

Clickable. Press Calculate, then change the facing and floor — the number, the band, the chart and the payback all move live. "Show me the shadows" is a button, not a gate.
Figures come from the real model in js/solar-api.js: $0.34/kWh SC-1, 3% escalation, 0.5% degradation, $1,200 mid-tier kit.

BLOCK CITY — the earlier static version, kept for comparison
Same look, but each block's tint is fixed: it comes from how open that block's sky is. That is a real consequence of the coastline, yet it reads as though each block's brightness were its solar output, which nobody has computed. Superseded by Sun City on its left.

PUBLIC RECORD — the closest to nyc.gov
Navy bar, Helvetica furniture, a statutory notice box, sources printed on the page. The affiliation disclaimer becomes designed furniture at the very top, which is both honest and exactly the register.
Tradeoff: municipal enough that some readers will assume it IS the city. That top strip is doing a lot of work.

STANDARDS MANUAL — Vignelli, not nyc.gov
Black, white, Helvetica, thick rules, the facts as a ruled table. The city in solid black is the strongest image of the three, and one red square carries the whole legal warning.
Tradeoff: no colour system left over. Results, charts and states all have to be invented later.

OPEN DATA — the portal register
Split screen: the city on the left, a worked estimate on the right. The only one showing a number before you type, and the only one whose map colour carries real data (borough).
Tradeoff: reads as a dashboard rather than a home page. Weakest hero of the three.

ON THE BLOCKS BEING REPRESENTATIVE
The geometry is real and unchanged: every square is rasterised from the city's published borough boundary files, at square ground cells. A rectangular cell was tried and dropped — it implies a street orientation that is only correct in part of Manhattan.
The per-block SHADING is gone. The dark Block City version tinted blocks by how open each block's sky is; that is a real consequence of the coastline but it is not model output, and it read as though it were. Doing it properly needs building heights for every lot, and NYC Open Data is blocked from this environment. So these three show the city plain, and every number on them is either published or computed by the site's own model. Open Data states the gap in a [NOT BUILT] box rather than filling it.

SUN CITY — the shaded blocks, lit by a sun that follows you
Move your cursor and the sun walks the sky; the city relights under it and the clock keeps up. Right is east and morning, left is west and evening, because the map is north-up. Left alone it drifts on its own until you touch it.
This also settles the honesty problem the static version had. The tint is no longer pretending to be per-block output — it is plainly light, and it moves, so nobody can read it as data. The blocks stay real; the number still comes from your address.
Cheap to run: all 5,141 blocks are one SVG path filled from a single radial gradient, so relighting the whole city is two attribute writes a frame, not five thousand.
